title: Simulated Annealing & Beam Search
html:
Simulated annealing is hill climbing that sometimes accepts a worse move — often early on, rarely later — so it can shake itself out of local optima. Beam search keeps several states instead of one.

The name comes from metallurgy: heating metal and cooling it slowly lets atoms settle into a low-energy crystal. The algorithm picks a random neighbour; if it is better it always moves, and if it is worse by ΔE it moves with probability:

P(accept worse move) = e^(−ΔE / T)

The temperature T starts high (random walk) and decreases according to a schedule (e.g. T ← 0.99·T). As T → 0 it becomes plain hill climbing. If T is lowered slowly enough, it finds the global optimum with probability approaching 1.

Local beam search

Keep k states instead of one. Each step, generate all successors of all k states and keep the best k overall. Unlike k independent restarts, information is shared: states on a good hill attract the whole beam.

Local beam search

Deterministic: top-k of all successors. Risk: the beam collapses into one small region (lack of diversity).

Stochastic beam search

Choose k successors at random, weighted by value — keeps diversity. Resembles natural selection, leading to genetic algorithms.

Beam search in NLP

The same idea decodes text from a language model: keep the k most probable partial sentences at each step (see Generative AI).

Watch out

The cooling schedule is the hard part: too fast and it freezes in a local optimum like hill climbing; too slow and it wastes time as a random walk. Tune the start temperature so early acceptance of worse moves is high (~80%).

How does simulated annealing escape local optima?

It accepts worse moves with probability e^(−ΔE/T). At high temperature many downhill moves are accepted (exploration); as T falls, it accepts fewer and settles into a good optimum (exploitation).

Local beam search vs k random restarts?

Restarts run independently. Beam search pools all successors and keeps the best k, so effort moves to the most promising regions — faster, but prone to losing diversity.
